extracted.intended_audience: government lawyers, Corps of Engineers officers, and officials administering river and harbor improvements
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and interpretive rules governing United States river and harbor improvement projects, including appropriation use, land acquisition/disposition, liabilities, property accountability, and the authority of the Secretary of War and various commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of river and harbor work as civil
rubrics_metrics.description: Work done by the United States upon rivers and harbors is civil work; assignment of military officers to such work does not make it military service and civilians employed on improvements are not 'in the employ of any branch of the military service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the work is civil and paid from civil appropriations, provisions of Army Regulations (e.g., paragraph 808, Army Regulations of 1889) were held not applicable to civilians on such projects; but the Secretary of War has discretionary power to require reports under other regulations (paragraph 569 of 1895 / 648 of 1901). (C. 147 Aug. 1894; C. 34-18 Aug. 1897.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of Corps officers from project appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers of the Corps of Engineers, when on duty solely connected with river and harbor improvements, may (and where permanent legislation, 'may' should be considered mandatory) be paid their pay and commutation of quarters from the appropriation for the work upon which employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proviso in permanent legislation increasing the Corps should be regarded as permanent; use of permissive 'may' in such context is to be considered mandatory so that officers engaged must be paid from the project appropriation. (C. 28632, June 27, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursement authority when appropriation grouped in same act
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appropriation for an investigation or project appears along with other appropriations in the same river and harbor act whose expenditure is under the Chief of Engineers, it should be disbursed by the Engineer Department under the general provision applying to other appropriations made by the same act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the specific item makes no express provision on the subject, the placement with other Chief-of-Engineers-directed items implies disbursement by the Engineer Department; the Secretary of War may direct such disbursement. (C. 3900, Feb. 25, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's authority to apply appropriations economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 of the river and harbor act (Aug. 11, 1888) empowers the Secretary of War to apply appropriated moneys 'by contract or otherwise as may be most economical and advantageous to the Government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authorizes actions such as hiring without formal contract for necessary services (example: hiring a steamboat to transport materials for levee protection), when such hiring is most economical/advantageous. (P. Jfi, 95, Mar. 1890; C. 15488 Nov. 9, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor obstruction of navigation — necessity and liability
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor engaged upon river and harbor work for the Government may obstruct navigation to the extent necessary to do his work, if such obstruction cannot reasonably be avoided; but he is civilly and criminally liable for any unauthorized obstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Secretary of War lacks authority to relieve the contractor from such liability for unauthorized obstruction. (C. 3839, Feb. 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on land acquisition authority (section 3736 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No land shall be purchased on account of the United States except under a law authorizing such purchase; the Secretary of War's authority to condemn, purchase, or accept donations applies only to works 'for which provision has been made by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of an appropriation for the works or express congressional authority, the Secretary is precluded by section 3736 from acquiring lands for river and harbor improvements; 'purchase' construed legally to include every mode of acquiring land other than by descent. (C. 3896 Feb. 1898; C. 2111 Mar. 1896; C. 11024 Aug. 1901; C. 13586 Nov. 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for lands flooded by river and harbor improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners of lands flooded by dams constructed in improving navigation are entitled to compensation for damages sustained by such flooding; the Secretary of War has authority under the April 24, 1888 act to purchase such lands or the right to flood them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When springs are located on such lands, their presence may properly be considered in determining the amount to be paid. (C. 1074, Mar. 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect of state grants creating rights for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A state grant to the United States (e.g., right to raise water level) may create a perpetual easement or servitude for the purposes specified, making subsequent conveyances of shore lands subject to that easement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if grantees later treat the grant as revocable license, courts/officials may treat it as a perpetual servitude binding later owners; notices of revocation may still be acknowledged. (C. 26425 Mar. 26, 1910; C. 20959 Mar./May 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Leasing vs. purchase — leasing limited by appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may acquire land/right of way/material by purchase or condemnation when provision is made by law; however, he cannot lease land unless an appropriation exists to pay the rental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquisition authority exists only when provision is made by law; leasing requires appropriation to cover rents. (C. 301 Sept. 1894; C. 195 Aug. 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government liability for damages from public works cannot be abrogated by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not within Congress's constitutional power to enact that the United States shall not be liable for damages caused by the prosecution of a public work; such a statute would be unconstitutional if it attempts to deprive third parties of property rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If liability would exist in the absence of a statute, a statute providing no liability would be an unconstitutional deprivation of property rights. (P. 56, 478 and 445, Dec. 1892.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Landowner remedies against U.S. representatives for occupied lands
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of lands occupied by a canal constructed as an improvement under a river and harbor act may, following precedent (U.S. v. Lee), maintain actions of ejectment or trespass against the official representative of the United States in charge of the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where works are federal improvements, private owners may bring common-law remedies against officials acting in possession. (P. 35, 191, Sept. 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of licenses in lieu of title acquisition for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriations are available for improvements (e.g., constructing a levee), work may proceed upon obtaining licenses from landowners without acquiring title to the underlying lands; section 355 R.S. has not been regarded as forbidding such improvements without title acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining revocable or other licenses can be a lawful substitute for purchasing title when appropriations authorize the work. (C. 13680 Nov. 25, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions precedent in appropriations — project as entirety
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appropriation for an improvement is conditioned upon specified acts (e.g., extinguishment of power rights by a State), the project is to be treated as an entirety and unless the conditions are satisfied the War Department cannot proceed with any part of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question may arise whether prior Government reliance on state action makes later rescission ineffective; Attorney General later held earlier state action could be substantial compliance, allowing Federal execution of authorized work. (C. 28390 May 22, 1911; AG opinions July 3, 1911 and Apr. 26, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of lands acquired for river and harbor improvements (section 5, 1902 act)
rubrics_metrics.description: When land acquired for river and harbor improvement is no longer needed, it may be sold 'in such manner as the Secretary of War may direct' and proceeds credited to the appropriation for the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation distinguishes 'purchase' (voluntary sale acquisition) from 'acquire' (donation or condemnation); lands merely segregated from the public domain should be returned to Interior rather than sold. Congress intended sale authority to eliminate property useless for the procurement's purpose without diminishing provisions for particular improvements. (C. 12479 Mar. 1, 1915.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures and scope for sale of unneeded lands
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary of War may sell certain lands not needed for projects (examples given: Dam No. 5, Yuba River settling basin) and may convey condemned land by warranty deed; sales may be tendered to highest bidder with deposit forfeiture provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where amount does not exceed specified small sums or matter is routine, Chief of Engineers may be authorized to permit sale; conveyance form may be adapted to transaction. (C. 13432 Oct. 21, 1902; C. 28349 May 9, 1911; C. 26472 Mar. 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary transfer of property and project credits/debits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under authority to apply appropriations economically and section 5 (1902), the Chief of Engineers may permit temporary transfer of property between projects upon equitable adjustment of charges and credits agreed upon by local engineer officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers between projects and sale of unserviceable property (where amount small, e.g., under $500) may be routine exercises of authority. (C. 16202 Apr. 20, 1904; C. 16336 Feb. 18, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and disposal of recovered/abandoned materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials (e.g., timber/logs) recovered in carrying on harbor work that have been abandoned and cannot be traced to owners are treated as belonging to the United States and may be used for the project; if not needed or serviceable, they may be sold under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recovered sticks of timber and sawed logs in Mobile harbor recovered after 30+ days without marks — treated as abandoned and usable/salable. (C. 15651 Dec. 18, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'military stores' and public property used for civil works
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'military stores' does not include public property purchased in carrying out civil works of river and harbor improvements; property-accountability regulations were intended to cover all public property under Secretary of War control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the President may sell military stores under section 1241 R.S., that term excludes civil-work property; regulation modifications could authorize engineer officers to drop non-military stores from returns upon certificate of wear, worthlessness, and destruction in their presence. (C. 3419 Aug. 1897.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's authority to permit use of land by license or lease
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may permit use of land under his control by revocable license or by lease under the act of July 28, 1892; lands not required for public use may be leased or sold under section 5 (1902).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protests that leasing a frontage imposes an undue burden on commerce (by favoring abutting owners) are without merit; if lands not required they may be leased or sold as provided. (O. 241 Aug. 1896; O. 19015 Jan. 4, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on subordinate commissions' authority over appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions such as the Mississippi River Commission derive no authority from their statutes to make allotments of moneys appropriated by Congress; their province is to recommend needed improvements and suggested appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allotments by such commissions are treated by the Secretary of War as recommendations only; the Secretary must not omit any works specially designated by Congress in appropriations. (P. 113, 187, Oct. 1890.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of maps and public circulation of commission outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps prepared by commissions under congressional appropriation may legally be disposed of at the commission's discretion; Congress intended such information to be made public and circulated for public use and benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission-produced informational materials are properly disseminated for public benefit. (P. 55, 326, July 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of duties and chain of command for river commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of bodies like the Missouri River Commission (composed partly of civilians) relate to specific work other than establishing harbor lines; as a body they are not subject to the directions of the Secretary of War in establishing harbor lines, and civilian members are not individually subject to his orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While commissions may consent to establish harbor lines, it is preferable for the Secretary to have such work done through Army engineer officers. (P. 56, 218, Oct. 1892.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and subsistence allowances for civilian commission members
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowances for traveling expenses of civilian members of commissions are fixed by statute and represent reimbursement of actual necessary outlay (not necessarily per diem); subsistence under authorized appropriations accrues only to members and authorized assistants/employees (not to wives/guests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mississippi and Missouri River Commission travel allowances governed by statute (P. U 477 Jan. 1891; C. 17890 Apr. 29, 1905); subsistence under the Apr. 28, 1904 appropriation limited to members and authorized personnel (C. 17890 Apr. 29, 1905).
